title: Lesson 1 Quiz: Income Distribution and Inequality
description: A short quiz to check what you learned in this lesson. Submitting it completes the lesson's quiz requirement, and your score is recorded separately.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not yet reviewed by a human (admin); do not give to students.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In Country K, every household's income rises by exactly 10% in one year, and prices do not change. What happens to the quintile income shares and to the number of people below a fixed poverty line?

choices.text: Income shares become more equal, and poverty stays the same
Income shares become less equal, and poverty falls
Income shares stay the same, and poverty may fall
Income shares become more equal, and poverty falls

questions.prompt: On a Lorenz curve, what does the point (60%, 30%) tell you?

choices.text: The poorest 60% of households together receive 30% of total income
The richest 60% of households together receive 30% of total income
The third quintile on its own receives 30% of total income
Incomes need to rise 30% for 60% of households to escape poverty

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Country L's quintile income shares, from poorest to richest, are 4%, 9%, 16%, 24%, and 47%. Using the trapezoid method for equal-sized quintiles, G ≈ 1 − Σ (Xₖ − Xₖ₋₁)(Yₖ + Yₖ₋₁), estimate the Gini coefficient. (Enter a decimal rounded to three decimal places, with no unit.)
Why does a Gini coefficient calculated from quintile shares usually understate inequality compared with one calculated from every household's income?

choices.text: Quintile tables leave the richest 5% of households out of the total
The trapezoid method counts the poorest quintile's income twice
Quintile data describe wealth, which is more equal than income
It treats the incomes inside each quintile as if they were equal

questions.prompt: Which statement about the causes of rising income inequality matches the lesson?

choices.text: Technology is the proven single cause, so other explanations are ruled out
Several factors are proposed, and economists debate how much each matters
Inequality rises mainly because the poverty line is raised each year
Changes in household structure have no effect on household inequality
